Name: feature_redundancy_tabular_robustness
Title: Feature Redundancy, Not Model Capacity, Drives Adversarial Robustness in Tabular Data
Short Hypothesis: The robustness of tabular classifiers to feature perturbations is primarily determined by the degree of feature redundancy (correlation), not model capacity. High feature redundancy allows perturbations to be compensated by other features, reducing attack success rates even for high-capacity models.
Related Work: Existing work on tabular adversarial robustness focuses on developing attacks (e.g., Ballet et al., 2019; Cartella et al., 2021) or defenses like adversarial training, often comparing model families on benchmark datasets. While some studies note that tree-based models can be robust to certain perturbations, the underlying data properties driving robustness remain unexplored. Our work is the first to systematically isolate feature redundancy as a causal factor using controlled synthetic experiments, distinguishing from model-centric approaches and providing a simple, data-centric explanation.
Abstract: Adversarial robustness in tabular data is typically studied through the lens of model architecture and attack strength. We propose and test a different hypothesis: that the robustness of tabular classifiers to feature perturbations is primarily governed by the degree of redundancy among features, rather than by model capacity. When features are highly correlated, a perturbation to one feature can be offset by others, making it harder for an attacker to flip the label. We conduct a controlled study using synthetic datasets with varying levels of feature correlation, training three model families of increasing capacity—regularized logistic regression, random forest, and a small multilayer perceptron—and subjecting them to three perturbation strategies: random noise, greedy single-feature flips, and gradient-based perturbations. We measure attack success rate and clean accuracy drop as a function of perturbation budget. Our experiments show that as feature redundancy increases, attack success rates drop significantly for all models, and the performance gap between low- and high-capacity models narrows. We validate these findings on several small real-world tabular datasets by measuring feature correlation and observing a similar trend. This work offers a simple, data-centric explanation for tabular adversarial robustness, suggesting that feature selection and data collection practices that promote redundancy can be a low-cost defense. All experiments run on a single CPU in under ten minutes, ensuring reproducibility in resource-constrained settings.
Experiments:
1. Synthetic data generation: Create datasets with N=1000 samples and d=10 continuous features drawn from a multivariate Gaussian with varying pairwise correlation ρ ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9}. Generate binary labels via a logistic function of a random subset of features to ensure learnability. Split 80/20 train/test.
2. Models: Train (a) L2-regularized logistic regression, (b) random forest (100 trees), (c) a small MLP (one hidden layer of 64 units, PyTorch) on each dataset. All training on CPU.
3. Attacks: (a) Random Gaussian noise with L∞ budget ε ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5} in standardized feature space. (b) Greedy single-feature perturbation: for each test instance, compute local sensitivity via finite differences (or gradients for differentiable models), select the feature with highest sensitivity, and perturb it by ε in the direction that most reduces the correct-class margin. (c) Gradient-based FGSM for logistic regression and MLP. Measure attack success rate (ASR) and clean accuracy drop.
4. Analysis: Plot ASR vs. ρ for each model and attack. Compute the average pairwise feature correlation and test its relationship with ASR using linear regression. Assess whether the ASR gap between models shrinks as ρ increases.
5. Real data validation: Use 2–3 small public tabular datasets (e.g., Iris, Wine, Breast Cancer) with <10000 rows and <50 features. Compute feature correlation, train the same models, apply the attacks, and check if higher correlation predicts lower ASR.
6. (Optional) Low-compute adversarial training: For the MLP, perform FGSM-based adversarial training (10% of training data) and evaluate whether it changes the redundancy-robustness relationship.
Metrics: Attack success rate, clean accuracy, robustness gap (clean accuracy minus accuracy under attack). Use 3 random seeds and report mean and standard deviation. Ensure each full experiment completes in under 10 minutes on a single CPU core.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Synthetic data may not fully capture real tabular complexities such as categorical features, missing values, and heterogeneous feature types. The correlation measure may not capture non-linear redundancy. Attack strength is limited by compute budget (few iterations, small ε grid), potentially underestimating vulnerability. Real datasets may have limited variation in feature correlation, requiring careful selection or augmentation. The label function in synthetic data must be controlled to avoid confounding with correlation. Results may be sensitive to normalization and feature encoding choices. The study does not aim to propose a state-of-the-art defense, but rather to provide a causal explanation; thus, practical deployment implications should be drawn cautiously.
